# The Times We Reach For It

> "Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest."
>
> — Matthew 11:28

The Big Monster isn't one lie. He's a pile of small ones, and each is attached to a particular moment in your day: "it helps me when I'm stressed", "it's the only way I get to sleep", "it's my reward".

A man who quits by willpower leaves that pile standing. He stops doing it but goes on believing in it. So every bad day and every sleepless night he feels robbed. Sooner or later he goes back for what he thinks is his. So we're going to take the pile apart, one occasion at a time, and you'll see where you've been getting robbed.

First, a word about fear, because fear and the lies work as a team. What does a strong urge actually feel like? You get a tight chest and restless hands, your mind won't settle, and you can't sleep. Now think where else you've felt exactly that. You felt it outside an exam hall, before a job interview, and walking over to speak to a girl you liked. It's anxiety. Most of what you call "the urge" is the fear of the urge, which is the dread that you'll be left wanting and miserable. The Little Monster only whispers. The fear is what makes it sound like a roar.

That's how men can still be pining a year after they stopped. Nothing in the body lasts a year. That part is all in the head.

## After a bad day {-}

Stress comes first, because for most men it's the big one.

I don't just mean life's disasters. I mean the ordinary grind. The boss's email arrives at ten to five. Then there's the bill you'd forgotten, the argument in the kitchen, the children screaming in the back of the car. Somewhere in the afternoon a thought slides in: *tonight, when everyone's in bed.* You haven't decided anything, and already you're leaning on it.

One man was honest enough to say he was sick of the whole arrangement:

> "I am fed up of constantly doing it under pressure and stress."
>
> — a commenter on a Christian recovery blog

Another man caught himself in the act of reaching for it, and saw what he was really after: "it's not that I'm horny I'm just depressed sad and I need dopamine". Thousands of men pressed the like button under that sentence. He added the line that explains half the habit: "I don't know how to handle being sad".

A psychiatrist who treats porn addiction says the same of the men who come to him: "people think that it's about sex. They think it's about lust. It's not. It's about emotional regulation." Don't hear that as an excuse. The lust is real, and Jesus named it. But lust is often only the shape the habit takes. What a man is using it for is to change how he feels.

Here is what is really going on. You're carrying two loads. One is the day's real trouble. The other is the Little Monster's low grumble, which you're so used to that you can't tell it from the first. When you do it, the second load lifts for a moment, so the total drops and you feel better. That lift is real. You haven't imagined it. But the email, the bill and the argument are all exactly where you left them. You've now added the flatness, a late night and one more broken promise. You're tenser than you'd have been if you'd never had the habit at all.

The habit gets the credit for easing a pressure that it largely built.

Then there's the word "reward". "I've worked hard, I've been good, I've earned it." One pastor has a warning for precisely that mood: "Never assume that you are above suffering or that you deserve relief through sin." A man on the NoFap forum, eight months free, wrote down the speech the Little Monster makes every evening: "You can stop tomorrow, but not today. Today you feel you deserve it." And look at the prize you're awarding yourself. One coach, who is no preacher, sums it up in five words: "Touching myself is not rewarding." He gives the reason elsewhere: "masturbation gives you the reward without the effort". A reward without the effort isn't a reward. It's a bribe, paid by the Little Monster to keep you where you are.

Here's a test. Have you ever expected the house to yourself for an evening and then had the plans change? Your wife's night out is cancelled, or a flatmate comes home early. Do you remember that flash of irritation, almost panic, far too big for what had happened? A free man doesn't get that. The habit put it there.

That's the truth about the habit and stress. It doesn't steady your nerves. It wears them down. Year after year it takes a little more of your courage, and all the while it tells you it's the only thing holding you together. One of the best things about getting out is that your natural confidence comes back. A man who isn't hiding anything walks into a room differently.

The verse that opens this chapter is an invitation to the tired and the loaded-down. It offers rest, and it doesn't send you off to earn it first. You've been taking your burdens to something that hands them back heavier.

## In bed with the phone {-}

If you're like most men, the phone is in your hand before your head has touched the pillow. What follows starts without any decision at all. It's second nature. Try to remember each time you did it last week. You'll recall one or two (the most recent, or the one you'd waited for) and the others have vanished. That's how little they meant.

"I do it when I'm bored." But boredom is a state of mind. Give a man something that absorbs him and he can go for days without a thought of it. Leave him flat on a bed with nothing to do and a screen full of half-dressed strangers. Now there's nothing between him and the Little Monster's whisper. He isn't bored and then tempted. He's itchy, and with nothing to distract him he notices it.

The psychiatrist from a moment ago puts this cue above all the dramatic ones: "number one cause of relapse is not actually strong negative emotion it is boredom". His reason takes one line: "if you've got a gap in your day porn will fill it".

The most famous fall in the Bible began in an empty hour. King David's army was away at war, and he had stayed at home. "At evening, David arose from his bed and walked on the roof of the king's house." He was idle, off duty and alone, and it was evening. You know that hour. You'll meet him again before the end of the book.

The bed, the phone and the closed door are just the cue from two chapters back. One man who now teaches other men about this noticed how little it had to do with desire: "you might not have even felt lustful at the time". It might be loneliness, he said, or just a certain time of night. His summary of his own cue was seven words long: "me having a phone by myself is problematic".

And far from curing boredom, the habit breeds it. Afterwards you're heavy and dull. You don't get up and ring a friend or fix the shelf. You lie there and scroll. The coach from a moment ago puts the cure for boredom the right way round: "When you stop escaping through porn, you get bored enough to actually build something." It's just as true of the habit without the porn, and of the hours spent messaging women you'll never meet. Boredom is what tells a man that he ought to be doing something, and the habit switches it off.

## "It clears my head" {-}

This is the opposite claim. Now the habit is supposed to help you concentrate.

You sit down to the essay, the tax return or the sermon you're meant to be preparing, and you're stuck. The itch is there too, nagging. So you "get it out of the way". The nagging stops, you go back to the desk, and the work gets done, and you conclude that it helped.

It didn't help. It removed a distraction that it had planted. The man who never had the habit sat down, got stuck, stayed in his chair and got unstuck. He had nothing to get out of the way.

What you actually bring back to the desk is a duller head. Men who stop say so again and again. One wrote: "Definitely improvement in focus and snappier information processing."

This occasion catches a lot of men who try willpower. They can put up with being irritable. But the first time they hit a blank at work they think, "If I could just clear my head the old way, I'd be fine." Watch how unfair the accounting is. While you had the habit, nothing was ever blamed on it. You were "tired" or "having an off day". The moment you stop, every blank is blamed on stopping.

Everybody gets stuck. When you're stuck and you do it, are you unstuck? No. So what do you do next? You do what the free man does and get on with it.

If you believe the habit helps you think, then worrying about its absence will guarantee you can't think. It's the doubt that causes the trouble. The itch doesn't.

## The shower and the quiet evening {-}

"It relaxes me."

Does it? Look at the thing itself. There's a locked door, and one ear is cocked for footsteps on the stairs. You delete the history and cover your tracks. In the shower you keep an eye on the clock, because people are waiting for the bathroom. A man who is relaxing doesn't behave like that. He looks like a burglar.

The morning shower deserves a mention, since so many of us start the day there. It's the loop again, in its purest form: warm water, a locked door, five minutes, the same as yesterday. Nothing in you asked for it. The shower asked for it.

Now take the evening. A man comes in from work, eats, puts his feet up, and he's content. The man with the habit can't be, quite. He has another appetite waiting, and until it's fed he's not fully in the room. He'll hurry the children's bedtime story. He'll be short with his wife for no reason she can find. He'll wait for the house to go to bed. Afterwards, for half an hour, he's as calm as other men are all evening.

Men call it the icing on the cake. It's a debt collector at the door.

Why is a free man relaxed without it? And why can't you relax after one or two days without? Read what men write in the first week of a white-knuckle "streak": pacing, snapping at people, counting the hours. That's what a man looks like when the single comfort he thinks he's entitled to has been taken away. He has forgotten what ordinary peace feels like.

It's like wading into a river. At first you're choosing every step and you could turn round whenever you like. Somewhere past the middle, you notice that the river has started doing the walking.

It's time to get out of the river.

## "I can't sleep without it" {-}

For many men this is the last one to fall, because the fear feels so practical. "I've got work in the morning. I can't lie awake."

So ask the plain questions. How did you sleep when you were eight? How do the men who've stopped sleep? How did you sleep in that tent, in that barracks, in your in-laws' spare room?

You've turned the last cue of the day into a sleeping pill. The bed is the cue. Lights out is the cue. So every night the Little Monster wakes up just as you lie down, and you can't settle until he's been fed. Then you sleep, and you thank the habit. It was the habit that kept you awake.

A psychiatrist describes the trick without any fuss: "you get the surge of dopamine you feel kind of content you feel a little bit sleepy so it's like it's almost like a self-medication." A medicine you need every night, for a restlessness the medicine causes, is not much of a medicine.

It's a poor sedative in any case. Ask this man:

> "I masturbate at night so i get tired because of which i am not able to wake early in the morning."
>
> — a commenter on a Christian recovery blog

The session runs late and the phone runs later, and at seven the next morning he drags himself out of bed and blames the mattress.

When you stop, you may have two or three nights when the old cue fires and you lie there for a while. Don't dread them. Lie there and smile, because you know what's dying. After that you'll sleep the way you did as a boy. David wrote of it: "In peace I will both lay myself down and sleep, for you, Yahweh alone, make me live in safety." (Psalm 4:8). Notice that he says he'll sleep in peace. He doesn't say he'll sleep worn out.

## Energy {-}

Most men know the flat ten minutes afterwards. Fewer notice what the habit does to their energy across years, because it happens so slowly.

It's like putting on weight. We look at a very heavy man and wonder how he let it happen. But suppose it happened in one night. You go to bed lean and fit, and you wake up five stone heavier, breathless on the stairs and aching in the knees. You'd be terrified. You'd be at the doctor's by nine. Yet it's the same condition whether it took one night or twenty years.

This is no different. Suppose I could lift you out of today and set you down three weeks after stopping. It would be just for a morning, so that you felt the difference all at once. That alone would do it. You wouldn't say, "Is this how good it gets?" You'd say, "Had I really sunk that far?"

I can't prove this to you with a lab report, and I won't pretend to. This is testimony. But the testimony is remarkably consistent:

> "First off, I finally have energy again! I haven't felt this good since high school."
>
> — a man on a NoFap forum, thirty days in

> "Motivation picked up too. I've gotten stuff done that I would have just let be in the past."
>
> — another man on a recovery site

Meanwhile the tiredness gets filed under "getting older". Your friends are tired too, so it seems normal. At twenty-eight you talk like a pensioner, and you assume that drive belongs to teenagers. Men even do it after the gym, the one hour of the day in which they built something up.

With the habit you're always drawing on the account. The good news is how fast the balance recovers. The path across the lawn takes a little while to grass over, but the fog starts lifting within days. That's on one condition, though. If you stop by willpower, feeling deprived, the gloom will swallow every gain. Stop this book's way and you get to enjoy them from the first morning.

I can't carry you three weeks forward. You can, though. You already know in your bones that it's true, because you remember being a boy.

## Before the date and after it {-}

Here's a piece of advice that men pass around as wisdom: take the edge off before you go out, so that you'll be relaxed with her and "not thinking with the wrong head".

Would you eat a full dinner at home before taking a girl to a restaurant? That's what you're doing. You arrive with the lights dimmed, a bit tired and a bit dull, missing the very spark that would have made you good company. A few nerves before a date are useful. They keep you sharp and they tell her that she matters. There's nothing to gain by drowning them.

Social occasions mix several of our reasons at once, because an evening out is stressful and relaxing at the same time. A long drive is the same: you have to concentrate for hours and you're bored stiff. And somewhere on the motorway the thought appears of what you'll do when you get home.

Then comes the other end of the evening. The date went badly, or it went nowhere. Or you had a row with your wife and she's gone to bed with her back to you. You come home with the particular ache of a man who's been turned down. Tonight of all nights, you tell yourself, you're owed something.

Look at what the habit offers. It's company that can't say no, because nobody is there. And each night you take that offer makes the real thing a little harder to face. A man who had been through it described where it leads:

> "I would stop talking to my friends my family I would just cut everything off and just isolate myself"
>
> — a young man telling his story on YouTube

A coach once took a call on his livestream from a man who was, by his own account, good at talking to women. He still couldn't stop retreating into fantasy when he should have been dating. The women in his head never turned him down, so he stayed there.

These are the nights you think you'd miss most. But they're the same principle. The habit quieted the Little Monster on a night when he happened to be loud. By doing so it made sure that he'd be loud on the next such night too.

## Loneliness {-}

Underneath most of the others lies this one.

You're alone in a flat or a hotel room, or you're lying beside a wife who feels a long way off. There is nobody to touch and nobody who knows you. And this, at least, feels like closeness.

It's the saddest of the lies, because the ache is real and it's a good ache. You were made for company. "It is not good for the man to be alone" is almost the first thing God says about us. Jason Evert, a Catholic speaker, passes on what a friend once told him: "What you really long for is authentic love, but you settled for the counterfeit." A psychiatrist says it in the language of chemistry: "you can't give oxytocin to yourself I can't hug myself I can't feel bonded to myself I require another human being".

A counterfeit doesn't only fail to pay. It makes you poorer. C.S. Lewis, answering a letter about this very habit, said it "sends the man back into the prison of himself, there to keep a harem of imaginary brides." Desire was meant to get you out of yourself. This locks you further in. Every time, you finish more alone than you began, in the same empty room with one more thing that nobody knows about you. The man from an earlier chapter who lost twenty years to it added a second cost to the first: "It also kept me isolated from real life". A secret is a wall. You're building it yourself, one evening at a time, between you and everyone who might have loved you. One coach says it in his own language: "You're losing your power, your essence to a phone screen."

Loneliness is also what breaks the men who quit by gritting their teeth. One man set himself a goal of five years and reached day 280. He had, in his own words, "even lost interest in porn". Then: "I ended up relapsing because I was overwhelmed by extreme loneliness and the feeling that nothing in my life was going right." The porn had gone, and the belief was still standing: that when a man is lonely enough, this is where he goes. That belief is the Big Monster, and no number of days will starve it. It has to be seen through.

A pastor, preaching on temptation, described what the bargain delivers. He was talking about porn, and every word fits the habit underneath it: "it promises the thrill and the relief, and it gives it to you for a moment, followed by depression and you feel even more alone than you did in the first place."

Loneliness is a hunger for people, and the habit feeds it a photograph.

## It's the occasion, not the habit {-}

So here's the list: the bad day, the empty hour, the stuck page, the quiet evening, the sleepless night, the nervous date, the lonely room. In every one of them the habit claimed to help. In every one it did no more than quiet, for a few minutes, a restlessness it had caused. Then it handed back your trouble with interest.

Get this clear. It was never the habit that made those moments bearable. The evening off, the warm shower and the clean bed are good in themselves, and the habit was a tax on them. Take away the need for it, and the good times get better and the hard times get easier.

A man who believes he needs this to cope will reach for it every time life leans on him. Such a man can't be trusted with much, least of all by himself. A man who knows he doesn't need it has nothing left to reach for.

Come to me, the verse says, and I will give you rest. That's better than relief, and you already know the difference between the two. Relief is what you've been buying every night for years, and it has never lasted till morning.
